title: Input resolution for detecting tampered card readers on a 2 GB device
body: Running a small detector on cheap cameras at payment points to flag a reader with something stuck over the keypad. The model works at 640 pixels on the long edge, but the device is a 2 GB ARM board and inference takes 900 ms. At 416 it takes 380 ms and recall on small overlays drops from 0.94 to 0.81. Do I crop to the keypad region at higher resolution, accept the lower recall, or add a second pass only when the first one is unsure?

comments.body: From the security side, recall on small overlays matters more than speed. A missed tamper is the costly mistake, an extra look is cheap. Do the crop at high resolution, the keypad does not move.
The keypad does move slightly between installs, and some cameras sit at an angle. So I would need a fixed region per device, calibrated once at installation.

Then calibrate once at install time, store the region per device and re-check if the camera view changes a lot. Cheaper than running the large model all the time. No be small thing to get right, but worth it.
A per-device region needs a way to update it remotely. Think about how that config is delivered, and what happens when a camera gets bumped and the region now points at the wall.
Two passes is a common design. Run 416 on every frame and only run the 640 crop when the first pass sees a change from the previous frame. Check how often that triggers in a day.
Quantise before you give up on resolution. Int8 on the same 640 model can cut inference time roughly in half on ARM, and then you can measure the recall loss, usually small, against the 416 loss.
Related: watch the cameras' auto exposure at night. If an overlay is only clear in daylight frames, recall in the evening will be lower than in your benchmark.

body: In our scraped Hausa text, 31 percent of the tokens that should contain ɓ, ɗ or ƙ had b', d' and k' or plain b, d and k instead, depending on the keyboard. Wrote a Python normaliser that maps the apostrophe forms back, and uses a word list to restore plain forms when the word has only one valid spelling. Most were recovered. The ambiguous ones stay as they are.

comments.body: How do you handle the word list following a standard that the scraped text does not? Dialect spelling and brand names would not be in it, and you might over-correct.
Maybe keep a counter of every correction and review the top fifty by hand each month. A cheap safeguard against a rule that silently damages one popular word.
Are you normalising to NFC? Hooked letters have precomposed forms, but I have seen text with a combining mark that looks identical and breaks lookups on the page.
Do you keep the original text next to the cleaned one? When the normaliser changes you want to rerun it from the source, not from the already cleaned version.
Seconding that. Store the raw version and a version number of the cleaning code. Rerunning from cleaned text compounds mistakes.
From the mobile side, many people type the apostrophe versions because the default keyboard has no hooked letters. A custom keyboard layout would improve the data at the source.
It also changes your model's input: a model trained only on cleaned text may meet the apostrophe forms at inference when people type like that. Keep some of the noisy forms in training.
Is the 31 percent evenly spread or from a few sources? If three websites account for most of it, fixing those at ingestion is easier than fixing the text later.
A word list will over-correct names too. Names such as Ɗanladi are written both ways in the wild and the list has no entry for them, so they should be left alone.
Out of curiosity, how many tokens is the corpus? I wonder whether 31 percent holds on a bigger scrape.
Yes, everything goes to NFC first. It was the first thing I checked, because a combining-mark version had split a few of my counts in two.
Ideally the raw files are immutable and the pipeline writes cleaned output with the version in the file name. Then comparing two versions of the cleaning is a diff of two folders.
Do you know of a keyboard layout people really use for Hausa? Our users in Côte d'Ivoire type Baoulé names and have the same trouble with open o and open e.

body: Our fine-tuning container ran as root and wrote checkpoints into a mounted volume, so everything came out owned by root and the next stage could not clean or move them without sudo. Added a user with the host UID in the Dockerfile and passed --user at run time. A small thing, but it had been annoying people for three months.

comments.body: Did you also point the Hugging Face cache at the mounted volume? Ours re-downloaded 4 GB of weights on every fresh container until we set HF_HOME to a volume.
Same with pip caches in CI builds. Anything large that the container fetches should live on a volume or a build cache, otherwise you pay for it on every run.

--user works until a library tries to write in the home directory and there is none. Set HOME to a writable path as well, or you get odd permission errors from tools that never mention the home folder.

body: Added npm audit --omit=dev to the pipeline with a failure threshold of high and above. Before, the step failed on everything including moderate issues in a build tool, so everyone ignored it and the real ones disappeared in the noise. Last week it caught a high severity issue in a body parser dependency, and for the first time the team fixed it the same day.

comments.body: Moderate in a dev dependency is mostly noise, but the omit-dev filter hides things too. A compromised build tool runs in your CI with your secrets. I would still read the full list weekly.
Weekly reading of a list nobody owns does not happen in practice. I would rather have a bot that opens a merge request for each update and let the pipeline run on it.
A bot opening ten merge requests a week is its own noise. Group the updates into one weekly request and merge when the pipeline is green.
Bots are fine for updates, but advisories are not only about updates. Some have no fix yet and need a decision, like replacing the package. That needs a human.
Both. The bot handles routine updates and the pipeline threshold stops the rest. The mistake is believing either one alone is enough.

body: L'étape de lint de notre pipeline mettait 3 minutes, dont 2 pour installer Cypress, qui télécharge un binaire de 200 Mo même quand on ne lance aucun scénario. Avec CYPRESS_INSTALL_BINARY=0 dans cette étape seulement, le lint passe à 50 secondes. Les étapes qui ont vraiment besoin du navigateur gardent l'installation normale.

comments.body: Pense à mettre le binaire en cache pour les étapes qui en ont besoin, dans le dossier de cache de Cypress. Sinon tu télécharges 200 Mo à chaque pipeline.
Même idée pour Puppeteer et son Chromium, avec PUPPETEER_SKIP_DOWNLOAD. Je l'ai appris quand le transfert sortant du serveur de CI a explosé.

title: Clinic data isolation in Postgres: row-level security, app filters or schemas
body: Hospital records API in Python on Postgres, now serving 40 clinics with about 6 million visit rows. Each clinic must see only its own patients. Options: row-level security with SET LOCAL app.clinic_id on each request, filtering in every query in the application code, or a schema per clinic. App filters are what we do today, and one forgotten WHERE in a report endpoint last month showed another clinic's counts for an hour. The team is three people, migrations must stay simple, and an auditor will ask how isolation is enforced.

comments.body: How does the clinic id reach the database, from the token on each request? On another backend I saw the tenant id passed by hand to every function, and it only takes one endpoint where somebody forgets it.

From the JWT claim: a dependency opens the transaction and runs SET LOCAL app.clinic_id before anything else. SET LOCAL, not SET, since connections are pooled and a plain SET would leak into the next request.

Two more traps with RLS: the table owner bypasses the policies unless you use FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY, and your app should connect with a role that is neither owner nor superuser. Migrations run as a different role.
Does SET LOCAL survive if the ORM opens a new transaction for a later query in the same request? Ours does that with autocommit in some paths, and I would not know until data went missing.
Schema per clinic with 40 clinics means each migration runs 40 times, plus search_path handling in the pooler. Fine at 40, at 400 it becomes a project. RLS keeps one set of tables.
What happens to query plans? current_setting in a policy can stop the planner from using an index if the column types differ. Check EXPLAIN on the heaviest report before committing.
I would keep the app filter as well. RLS is the backstop and the filter keeps queries explicit and readable. Two layers, and an auditor likes that you did not rely on one.
RLS policies are SQL you can show an auditor on one page. App filters are scattered across the codebase, so proving isolation means reading all of it.
Do clinics ever share patients, like referrals to a bigger hospital? That breaks the clean partition. Whatever you choose, plan how one record becomes visible to two clinics.
Think about the screens that cross clinics, like a district health officer's overview. Those need a role that sees everything, and the interface should make it obvious which scope you are in.
On the mobile side, check what is cached on the phone when a user moves from one clinic to another. The isolation in Postgres does not help if the app keeps the first clinic's list.
Schema per clinic has one advantage nobody mentioned: restoring a single clinic from backup is straightforward. With RLS you would restore into a side database and copy rows over.
I used RLS on a previous system. The surprise was that an UPDATE on a row you cannot see silently changes nothing, with no error, so code that assumes one row was updated needs to check the count.
That is a useful warning. Did it show up in your logs at all, or did you find out because a user complained?
RLS plus the app filter gets my vote. Keep it boring.
Give the audit table its own policy. Reviewers need to see the entries across all clinics, and every request must be able to insert into it regardless of its clinic scope.

body: Porting firmware to Rust on a small Cortex-M0+ with 32 KB of flash. The logic crate builds for the thumbv6m target in CI without trouble, but I cannot run the logic on the board from the pipeline. How do you check firmware logic in CI without hardware? Compile the logic crate for the host and run it there, use QEMU or Renode for the target, or keep a board attached to a runner? I would like a failing state machine transition to fail the merge request.
